subject: Problem with matrix identification for bifactor CFA on lavaan?

messages.author: c1e6fe5d79a18b6f
messages.subject: Problem with matrix identification for bifactor CFA on lavaan?
parts:
Hello,
I am trying to run a bifactor CFA. I have ~1440 samples with 6 DSM categories. I am using lavaan. For my model, I had:
> bifactor <- 'general =~c_dep_probs_ts + c_anx_probs_ts + c_somatic_probs_ts + c_adhd_probs_ts + c_odd_probs_ts + c_cd_probs_ts
internalizing =~c_dep_probs_ts + c_anx_probs_ts + c_somatic_probs_ts
externalizing =~c_adhd_probs_ts + c_odd_probs_ts + c_cd_probs_ts'
>modelfit <- cfa(model=bifactor, sample.cov=covaCBCL, std.lv = TRUE, orthogonal = TRUE)
>summary(modelfit,standardized= TRUE, rsquare = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE)

When I run this, I get:
"lavaan WARNING:
Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could
not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not
identified."

Is there a way to remedy this? When I run it on 1 factor, there is no issue, albeit poor fit. When I run it on 2 factors (i and e), it also works. I only run into this issue when I am having this 'overlap'.
The output I do get is fairly decent with respect to fit indices etc.

With regards to identification, I am not sure why it wouldn't be identified, since n(n+1) would yield 21.
Model Test User Model: Test statistic 22.948 Degrees of freedom 3 P-value (Chi-square) 0.000 Model Test Baseline Model: Test statistic 3831.453 Degrees of freedom 15 P-value 0.000 User Model versus Baseline Model: Comparative Fit Index (CFI) 0.995 Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI) 0.974 Akaike (AIC) 56129.762 Bayesian (BIC) 56224.640 Sample-size adjusted Bayesian (BIC) 56167.461 Root Mean Square Error of Approximation: RMSEA 0.068 90 Percent confidence interval - lower 0.044 90 Percent confidence interval - upper 0.095 P-value RMSEA <= 0.05 0.105 Standardized Root Mean Square Residual: SRMR 0.012 Thank you so much!

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: Problem with matrix identification for bifactor CFA on lavaan?
parts: You are missing the covariance between I and E factors

bifactor <- '
general =~c_dep_probs_ts + c_anx_probs_ts + c_somatic_probs_ts + c_adhd_probs_ts + c_odd_probs_ts + c_cd_probs_ts
internalizing =~c_dep_probs_ts + c_anx_probs_ts + c_somatic_probs_ts
externalizing =~c_adhd_probs_ts + c_odd_probs_ts + c_cd_probs_ts

internalizing ~~ externalizing
'

In a bifactor model, the general factor is not correlated with any other factor, but the specific factors are correlated between them

messages.subject: Re: Problem with matrix identification for bifactor CFA on lavaan?
parts:
I would say that if the model fit is good for the 2 factor solution, might be that the general factor is not a good model

Also, my bias is that I do not like the bifactor model in general. Seems theoretically weird to interpret for me

Can you present the output from the summary from that model?

Basically ML couldnt find a solution. In some other software I have seen starting values helping. But I havent seen that making a big difference with lavaan, as it is not very sensitive to it

This is running into the same type of issue as multi-trait multi-method models, which commonly run into this type of issues as you might be asking too much for a single item

messages.author: 12fdd832cacb825e
messages.subject: Re: Problem with matrix identification for bifactor CFA on lavaan?
parts:
One step further.

cfa() covaries all latents by default. So you also need:

general ~~ 0*externalizing + 0*internalizing

to identify the model.

Though looking at your content, it's a research area I'm familiar
with, and I'm skeptical a factor model is the way to go conceptually,
which could lead to estimation problems if the model is flat wrong.
But that's not really about lavaan.

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: Problem with matrix identification for bifactor CFA on lavaan?
parts:
I think that if you were to have more items it would most likely work

A note about the fit measures, be careful for the interpretation of the RMSEA, as it favours larger models, so its easy to trick it into showing better fit by simple adding more parameters.

Previous research has shown that CFI and Gamma-Hat are less sensitive to characteristics like this, and mainly be sensitive to model misfit.

Garnier-Villarreal, M., & Jorgensen, T. D. (2020). Adapting Fit Indices for Bayesian Structural Equation Modeling: Comparison to Maximum Likelihood. Psychological Methods, 25(1), 46–70. https://doi.org/dx.doi.org/10.1037/met0000224

Fan, X., & Sivo, S. A. (2007). Sensitivity of fit indices to model misspecification and model types. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 42(3), 509–529. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273170701382864


Now, my rant about the bifactor model. The reason I dont like is on how it is interpret, a basic constraint of the model is that the General factor is not correlated to the specific factors. So, as in your case you have externalization and internalization, for the model to make theoretical sense you would have to argue that the General factor is something that all the items share that is completely separate from externalization and internalization. Which then I dont understand how to make sense of that. Which for me its even weirder when use in Intelligence, as the have specific factors of cognitive performance (like executive function, visou-spatial, etc), and then set a General Intelligence factor, but if this general factor is uncorrelated to executive functions, how can I say that is Intelligence at all? For me these models make more theoretical sense as second order factors

Also, research has shown that the bifactor model simply fits better to random data, so it might just be a general factor structure that fits well without necessary being relevant (sorry I dont have those references at hand)

End rant

parts:
Hello,

I apologize for never responding. Thank you for sharing these references with me. I agree with your reasoning. I guess the reason why I am doing bifactor is that the intent is to compute a general factor and try to try and predict it via other variables (not mentioned) as well as to try and predict "disorder specific residuals," so bi-factor is more consistent in that way. I am not committed to it, though. 

I have a question, though, I went back and added 3 more groups. After I did EFA, it showed me that 4 factors work. 4 factors also converges acceptably in CFA, as does 1 general factor. Discarding the bifactor model, I still find that when I run with a general factor g and 4 individual factors, the model fails to find a solution. Is there anything that I am missing, or is this just a data issue?

factor <- 
' gen =~ RS_c_odd_probs_ts + RS_c_adhd_probs_ts + RS_c_somatic_probs_ts + RS_c_anx_probs_ts + RS_c_dep_probs_ts + RS_c_sct_ts + RS_c_ocd_probs_ts + RS_c_stress_probs_ts
  f1 =~ RS_c_anx_probs_ts + RS_c_ocd_probs_ts + RS_c_stress_probs_ts
  f2 =~ RS_c_odd_probs_ts + RS_c_adhd_probs_ts + RS_c_stress_probs_ts
  f3 =~ RS_c_dep_probs_ts + RS_c_somatic_probs_ts 
  f4 =~ RS_c_dep_probs_ts + RS_c_sct_ts'

lavaan WARNING: the optimizer warns that a solution has NOT been found!
Thank you so much,

On Friday, July 17, 2020 at 3:34:07 PM UTC-4 mauga...@gmail.com wrote:
I think that if you were to have more items it would most likely work

A note about the fit measures, be careful for the interpretation of the RMSEA, as it favours larger models, so its easy to trick it into showing better fit by simple adding more parameters.

Previous research has shown that CFI and Gamma-Hat are less sensitive to characteristics like this, and mainly be sensitive to model misfit.

Garnier-Villarreal, M., & Jorgensen, T. D. (2020). Adapting Fit Indices for Bayesian Structural Equation Modeling: Comparison to Maximum Likelihood. Psychological Methods, 25(1), 46–70. https://doi.org/dx.doi.org/10.1037/met0000224

Fan, X., & Sivo, S. A. (2007). Sensitivity of fit indices to model misspecification and model types. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 42(3), 509–529. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273170701382864


Now, my rant about the bifactor model. The reason I dont like is on how it is interpret, a basic constraint of the model is that the General factor is not correlated to the specific factors. So, as in your case you have externalization and internalization, for the model to make theoretical sense you would have to argue that the General factor is something that all the items share that is completely separate from externalization and internalization. Which then I dont understand how to make sense of that. Which for me its even weirder when use in Intelligence, as the have specific factors of cognitive performance (like executive function, visou-spatial, etc), and then set a General Intelligence factor, but if this general factor is uncorrelated to executive functions, how can I say that is Intelligence at all? For me these models make more theoretical sense as second order factors

Also, research has shown that the bifactor model simply fits better to random data, so it might just be a general factor structure that fits well without necessary being relevant (sorry I dont have those references at hand)

End rant




On Friday, July 17, 2020 at 12:43:47 AM UTC-5 Puzzled wrote:
I am leaning towards this conclusion as well. It is unfortunate because the EFA seemed quite promising but ah, well. 

Thank you both so much for your help!

It also may be, as Mauricio said earlier, that this is just the wrong
model for these data. I don't have much experience myself with
bifactor models, but you might be running into identification problems
with only two specific factors.
